title: History of Canada
wiki_lead:
The history of Canada covers the period from the arrival of the Paleo-Indians to North America thousands of years ago to the present day. The lands encompassing present-day Canada have been inhabited for millennia by Indigenous peoples, with distinct trade networks, spiritual beliefs, and styles of social organization. Some of these older civilizations had long faded by the time of the first European arrivals and have been discovered through archaeological investigations.
From the late 15th century, French and British expeditions explored, colonized, and fought over various places within North America in what constitutes present-day Canada. The colony of New France was claimed in 1534 by Jacques Cartier, with permanent settlements beginning in 1608. France ceded nearly all its North American possessions to Great Britain in 1763 at the Treaty of Paris after the Seven Years' War. The now British Province of Quebec was divided into Upper and Lower Canada in 1791. The two provinces were united as the Province of Canada by the Act of Union 1840, which came into force in 1841. In 1867, the Province of Canada was joined with two other British colonies of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia through Confederation, forming a self-governing entity. "Canada" was adopted as the legal name of the new country and the word "Dominion" was conferred as the country's title. Over the next eighty-two years, Canada expanded by incorporating other parts of British North America, finishing with Newfoundland and Labrador in 1949.
Although responsible government had existed in British North America since 1848, Britain continued to set its foreign and defence policies until the end of World War I. The Balfour Declaration of 1926, the 1930 Imperial Conference and the passing of the Statute of Westminster in 1931 recognized that Canada had become co-equal with the United Kingdom. The Patriation of the Constitution in 1982 marked the removal of legal dependence on the British parliament. Canada currently consists of ten provinces and three territories and is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy.
Over centuries, elements of Indigenous, French, British and more recent immigrant customs have combined to form a Canadian culture that has also been strongly influenced by its linguistic, geographic and economic neighbour, the United States. Since the conclusion of the Second World War, Canada's strong support for multilateralism and internationalism has been closely related to its peacekeeping efforts.

Indigenous peoples


Indigenous societies

Archaeological and Indigenous genetic evidence indicates that North and South America were the last continents into which humans migrated. During the Wisconsin glaciation, which began 100,000–75,000 years ago and ended about 11,000 years ago, falling sea levels allowed people to move gradually across the Bering land bridge (Beringia), from Siberia into northwest North America. At that point, they were blocked by the Laurentide ice sheet, then covering most of Canada, confining them to Alaska and the Yukon for thousands of years. The exact dates and routes of the peopling of the Americas are the subject of an ongoing debate. 
About 16,000 years ago, the glacial melt allowed people to move by land south and east out of Beringia, and into Canada. The Haida Gwaii islands, Old Crow Flats, and the Bluefish Caves contain some of the earliest Paleo-Indian archeological sites in Canada. Ice Age hunter-gatherers of this period left lithic flake fluted stone tools and the remains of large butchered mammals.
The North American climate stabilized around 8000 BC (10,000 years ago). Climatic conditions were similar to modern patterns; however, the receding glacial ice sheets still covered large portions of the land, creating lakes of meltwater. grok_lead: The history of Canada comprises the long-term inhabitation of its lands by diverse Indigenous peoples for at least 12,000 years before European contact, marked by complex societies, intergroup conflicts, and adaptations to varied ecologies from Arctic tundra to Pacific coasts. The earliest confirmed European incursion was a brief Norse outpost at L'Anse aux Meadows circa 1021 AD, evidencing transatlantic voyages but no lasting settlement. Sustained European engagement commenced in the 16th century through exploratory voyages, including John Cabot's 1497 landing under English commission and Jacques Cartier's 1534 expedition for France, which initiated claims to territories and fur trade networks along the Atlantic and St. Lawrence regions. French colonization established New France, centered on Quebec and Montreal, fostering alliances and rivalries with Indigenous nations amid resource extraction and missionary efforts, until imperial competition with Britain escalated into the Seven Years' War (1756â1763). The conflict's resolution via the Treaty of Paris in 1763 transferred French holdings in Canada to British sovereignty, integrating a Francophone population under the Quebec Act of 1774 and attracting American Loyalists fleeing post-Revolutionary persecution, thereby diversifying the colonial populace. British North America weathered the War of 1812 against U.S. expansionism, endured 1837â1838 rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada demanding democratic reforms, and navigated economic pressures from infrastructure deficits and U.S. proximity, culminating in the British North America Act of 1867. This legislation confederated the provinces of Canada (split into Ontario and Quebec), New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia into the Dominion of Canada on July 1, 1867, instituting a federal structure with parliamentary democracy under monarchical oversight, while reserving powers between central and provincial governments. Subsequent westward expansion via the Canadian Pacific Railway, acquisition of Rupert's Land, and provincial incorporations extended sovereignty to the Pacific and Arctic, fueling resource booms in timber, mining, and agriculture but displacing Indigenous groups through treaties often enforced asymmetrically. Canada 's autonomous contributions to the First and Second World Warsâdeploying over 1.1 million troops in the former and building the era's third-largest navy in the latterâenhanced international stature, spurred industrialization, and accelerated immigration, transforming the nation into a G7 economy with universal healthcare and bilingual policies amid ongoing federal-provincial tensions, particularly in Quebec.
